## Goals

By the end of this lab, you should

1. have an understanding of text versus binary files,
2. be able to distinguish between flat versus hierarchical file types, and
3. be able to load numeric data using [DelimitedFiles.jl](https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1.12/stdlib/DelimitedFiles/) or [CSV.jl](https://csv.juliadata.org/stable/).

## Data storage formats

- Files on a computer can be categorized as *text files* or *binary files*. Both file types are encoded as bit patterns.
- **Text files** encode individual characters, allowing *text editor programs* to easily display the contents of a file to a user.
    + *Examples*: CSV (`.csv`), TSV (`.tsv`), HTML (`.html`), XML (`.xml`), JSON (`.json`)
    + Often has a specific standard defining how these files are formatted; for example valid CSV files should adhere to [RFC 41800](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc4180/).
    + Internal markup language/syntax is fairly simple.
    + Usually, but not always, related to storing a dataset in the sense that is familiar to statisticians/data scientists.
- **Binary files** have their contents encoded in a (sometimes proprietary) specialized format. These types of files are typically *not meant* to be manipulated by text editors, and instead use their specialized representation to minimize file size or enhance performance in certain workflows.
    + *Examples*: [R data](https://www.r-bloggers.com/2021/12/how-to-read-rda-file-in-r-with-example/) (`.Rda` and similar file types), [Arrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apache_Arrow) (`.arrow`), [Parquet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apache_Parquet) (`.parquet`), [Python's Pickle format](https://docs.python.org/3/library/pickle.html) (`.pkl` or `.pickle`), [HDF5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hierarchical_Data_Format) (`.hdf5`), [JLD2](https://juliaio.github.io/JLD2.jl/stable/) (`.jld2`).
    + Who knows how the contents are stored... it does not matter for the intended use.
    + Often, but not always, related to the idea of *serializing objects* in a programming language so they can be reused across sessions.

## Text file types

### Flat text files

**Flat text files** are straightforward. Other than relying on a few special characters to separate distinct items, the textual representation you see exactly defines the data.

+ Common format for tabular data: 1 row = 1 observation and 1 column = 1 variable, field, or parameter.
+ Might rely on **fixed width format** in which each value must be encoded as text of a certain length.
+ Might rely on a **delimiter** to separate distinct values.

One annoying quirk: Windows and Linux-like systems use different line endings!

+ Line endings typically handled by invisible [ASCII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ASCII) characters.
+ If you create a file on Windows: newline `\n` and carriage return `\r`.
+ If you create a file on MacOS/UNIX/Linux: only newline `\n`.

### Hierarchical text files

Some text files rely on a **hierarchical structure** defined by an elaborate markup language.
A classic example is HTML:

- Usually starts with `<!DOCTYPE html>` as a document type declaration (if adhering to W3C standards).
- Followed by an opening `<html>` tag...
- Followed by a nested `<head></head>` section...
- Followed by a nested `<body></body>`...
- And finally closed out by an `</html>` tag.

We can edit these by hand, but its best to use a specialized editor to parse and edit, whenever possible.

## How to read and write

### Streams

Julia's support for powerful abstraction makes it so you can get by only knowing about the `open()` command $\pm$ 1 or 2 additional tools.
Specifically, the patterns you should commit to memory are:

```{julia}
#| eval: false
# to read a file
open("path/to/file", "r") do io
  # do something with the IO stream
end
```

```{julia}
#| eval: false
# to (over)write to a file
open("path/to/file", "w") do io
  # do something with the IO stream
end
```

In both instances, you are manipulating an `IOStream` object that handles the logic of reading and writing the contents of a file.
The patterns above ensure you always close out the underlying stream.
There are many convenience functions like `read()`, `readlines()`, and `write()` that you might also find helpful.

You've already been working with **streams**:

- `stdout`, the standard output stream. This is used to handle the logic of displaying information to you when you run commands in the Julia REPL.
- `stdin`, the standard input stream. This is used to handle the logic of reading and parsing commands you enter in the Julia REPL.

The following focuses on the DelimitedFiles.jl and CSV.jl packages.

### How to read a file

Using DelimitedFiles (part of the standard library):

```{julia}
using DelimitedFiles

mydata = readdlm("../hw/assets/nnmf-2429-by-361-face.txt")
mydata
```

- No header line.
- Not fixed-width as we can see violations of that format in the last few entries on both lines.
- Delimited, since a single space character, `' '`, is used to separate values.
- An invisible line ending is used to place rows on separate lines. Should be `'\n'`. Verify this on your own.
- The data happens to be numeric floating point numbers. Is `Float64` optimal here? Maybe we could get away with `Float32`...

**Even if a parser's heuristic defaults work, you should practice fully specifying how you load the data**:

```{julia}
using DelimitedFiles

mydata = readdlm("../hw/assets/nnmf-2429-by-361-face.txt", ' ', Float64; header = false)
mydata
```

- Same result.
- This approach documents what **we** relied on to parse the data into an appropriate Julia object.
- People living in the future will thank you for your benevolence.

Alternatively, we can use the combination of CSV.jl with Tables.jl to parse and import the data as a `Matrix{Float64}`:

```{julia}
#| eval: false
using CSV, Tables
mydata = CSV.read("../hw/assets/nnmf-2429-by-361-face.txt", Tables.matrix; header = false)
```

- Tables.jl: provides a specification for what "tabular data" means. The CSV.jl package uses it to some extent.
- CSV.jl: handles parsing a CSV file based on a careful definition of how these files are defined. Will work with other delimiters like tabs, `\t`, pipes `|`, and so on.
- Both of these packages have too many features to list here.

### How to write a file

Using DelimitedFiles.jl:

```{julia}
#| eval: false
using DelimitedFiles, Images

myitem = mydata[:, 1]
writedlm("whatisthis.txt", myitem, ' ')
```

Using CSV.jl + Tables.jl:

```{julia}
#| eval: false
using CSV, Tables

myitem = mydata[:, 1]
CSV.write("whatisthis.txt", Tables.table(myitem), delim = ' ', header=false)
```

- CSV expects the object to be saved to generate "rows". Since a `Vector{Float64}` iterates `Float64` values, CSV.jl will complain that your object is not a table.
- Wrap it in `Tables.table()` to specify a table-like structure. You use it to add a `header`.


## Handling file paths

Earlier you encountered the relative file path `"../hw/assets/nnmf-2429-by-361-face.txt"`.
This is bad because Windows and Linux-like systems use different file path separators.
The better, robust alternative is to use `joinpath()` to form paths:

```{julia}
joinpath("..", "hw", "assets", "nnmf-2429-by-361-face.txt")
```

This will $\text{Do The Right Thing}^{\text{TM}}$ depending on the underlying operating system.

Create a copy of the file `nnmf-2429-by-361-face.txt` named `nnmf-2429-by-361-face.dat`.
**Does changing the file extension change how DelimitedFiles or CSV interpret this file?**
Explain why you think this is the case.



### Question 2

Navigate to the UCI Machine Learning Repository page for the [Auto MPG](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/9/auto+mpg) dataset.
Download the [ZIP file](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ZIP_(file_format)) **and decompress it.**
You can do this any way you find suitable, but challenge yourself to do it all through our class Linux container.
**How can you load the `auto-mpg.data-original` file contained in the ZIP archive to Julia?**



### Question 3 (Optional)

Bundling files into archives (like ZIP or Tar) is a common and popular way to share files with others.
Often, this involves some compression to reduce file size and make transfers as fast as possible.
The [ZipArchives](https://github.com/JuliaIO/ZipArchives.jl) package provides an interface to working with the ZIP file format.

**Repeat the task in Question 2, operating directly on the ZIP file you downloaded.**
Use it to read `auto-mpg.data-original` directly from the ZIP file and correctly encode missing values as the `missing` type in Julia.
The [DataFrames](https://github.com/JuliaData/DataFrames.jl) can be useful for this purpose.
See the tutorial here: [https://csv.juliadata.org/stable/examples/#zip_example](https://csv.juliadata.org/stable/examples/#zip_example).



### Question 4 (Optional)

**In a simple step-by-step procedure, describe how you can create a ZIP archive to store several outputs generated by Some Fancy Algorithm.**
For the sake of this example, let's assume the outputs are all `Matrix{Float64}` objects.
